question: A developer is building a serverless application using AWS Lambda. The function needs to process messages from an Amazon SQS standard queue. The function occasionally fails due to downstream service timeouts. What should the developer configure to prevent the same message from being processed repeatedly while still ensuring no messages are lost?
choices: Increase the SQS visibility timeout to be at least 6 times the Lambda function timeout
Enable long polling on the SQS queue
Set the Lambda function reserved concurrency to 1
Configure the SQS queue as a FIFO queue
explanation_html:
Correct answer: Increase the SQS visibility timeout to be at least 6 times the Lambda function timeout

When Lambda reads a message from SQS, the message becomes invisible for the duration of the visibility timeout. If processing takes longer than the visibility timeout, the message reappears and can be processed again. AWS recommends setting the visibility timeout to at least 6 times the Lambda function timeout to allow for retries. Long polling reduces empty API calls but does not address duplicate processing. Setting concurrency to 1 creates a bottleneck. FIFO queues enforce ordering but do not resolve the timeout/duplicate issue.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/with-sqs.html

question: A developer needs to store session data for a web application with unpredictable traffic spikes. The data must be accessible with single-digit millisecond latency. Which DynamoDB capacity mode should the developer choose?
choices: Provisioned capacity mode with Auto Scaling enabled
On-demand capacity mode
Provisioned capacity mode with reserved capacity
Global tables with provisioned capacity
explanation_html:
Correct answer: On-demand capacity mode

DynamoDB on-demand mode instantly accommodates workload demands without capacity planning. It is ideal for unpredictable traffic and you pay per request. Provisioned with Auto Scaling can lag during sudden spikes. Reserved capacity suits stable, predictable workloads. Global tables address multi-region replication, not traffic spikes.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/HowItWorks.ReadWriteCapacityMode.html

question: A company exposes a REST API via Amazon API Gateway backed by Lambda. They want to limit requests per individual client to prevent abuse. Which feature should be used?
choices: API Gateway resource policies
API Gateway usage plans with API keys
AWS WAF integration with API Gateway
Lambda authorizers
explanation_html:
Correct answer: API Gateway usage plans with API keys

Usage plans define throttle and quota limits per API key, enabling per-client rate limiting. Resource policies control access at the API level. WAF provides IP-based rate limiting but is not designed for per-client key throttling. Lambda authorizers handle authentication, not rate limiting.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/apigateway/latest/developerguide/api-gateway-api-usage-plans.html

question: A team uses AWS CodeDeploy to deploy to EC2 instances. If the deployment fails, the application must automatically revert to the last good version. Which configuration achieves this?
choices: Configure a CloudWatch alarm and enable alarm-triggered rollback
Enable automatic rollback on deployment failure in the deployment group settings
Use in-place deployment with a custom rollback script in the AppSpec file
Set the minimum healthy hosts to 100% in the deployment configuration
explanation_html:
Correct answer: Enable automatic rollback on deployment failure in the deployment group settings

CodeDeploy supports automatic rollback when a deployment fails. Enabling this in the deployment group causes CodeDeploy to redeploy the last successful revision automatically. CloudWatch alarm rollbacks are for monitoring-based scenarios, not direct failure rollback. Custom scripts add complexity and are not built-in rollback. Setting minimum healthy hosts to 100% prevents some rollouts but does not configure rollback behavior.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/codedeploy/latest/userguide/deployments-rollback-and-redeploy.html

question: A developer is troubleshooting latency in a microservices app using Lambda, DynamoDB, and SQS. They need to identify which service is causing slowness. Which AWS service provides end-to-end distributed tracing?
choices: Amazon CloudWatch Logs Insights
AWS CloudTrail
AWS X-Ray
Amazon CloudWatch Metrics
explanation_html:
Correct answer: AWS X-Ray

AWS X-Ray provides end-to-end tracing of requests across distributed services, creating a visual service map with per-segment latency. It integrates natively with Lambda, DynamoDB, SQS, and API Gateway. CloudWatch Logs Insights queries log data but does not trace requests across services. CloudTrail records API calls for auditing. CloudWatch Metrics provides aggregate service metrics, not request-level distributed traces.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/xray/latest/devguide/aws-xray.html

question: A Lambda function needs to access a third-party API key securely. The key must be encrypted at rest and the function must retrieve it at runtime without hardcoding it. What is the recommended approach?
choices: Store the API key in a Lambda environment variable encrypted with the default Lambda service key
Store the API key in AWS Secrets Manager and retrieve it using the SDK at runtime
Hardcode the API key in the Lambda deployment package and rotate it monthly
Store the API key in an S3 bucket with server-side encryption and read it on startup
explanation_html:
Correct answer: Store the API key in AWS Secrets Manager and retrieve it using the SDK at runtime

AWS Secrets Manager is purpose-built for storing, rotating, and retrieving secrets. It encrypts secrets using KMS, supports automatic rotation, and provides fine-grained IAM access control. Lambda environment variables are encrypted at rest but do not support automatic rotation and are visible in the Lambda console. Hardcoding secrets is a security anti-pattern. S3 can store secrets but lacks the secret lifecycle management features of Secrets Manager.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/secretsmanager/latest/userguide/intro.html

question: A developer wants to share a common set of Python libraries (numpy, pandas) across multiple Lambda functions without including them in every deployment package. What is the best approach?
choices: Create a Lambda layer containing the libraries and attach it to each function
Upload the libraries to S3 and download them on each Lambda cold start
Include the libraries in every Lambda deployment package separately
Use an EFS mount to share the libraries across Lambda functions
explanation_html:
Correct answer: Create a Lambda layer containing the libraries and attach it to each function

Lambda layers allow you to package and share libraries, custom runtimes, or configuration files across multiple Lambda functions. Layers are extracted to /opt in the execution environment and are included in the deployment package size limit. Downloading from S3 on every cold start adds latency. Duplicating libraries in every package increases deployment size and maintenance burden. EFS is a valid option for very large dependencies but layers are simpler and the preferred approach for standard library sharing.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/configuration-layers.html

question: A DynamoDB table stores order data. Queries frequently filter by customerId (partition key) and need to sort results by orderDate. Sometimes queries also filter by orderStatus. Which index design is most efficient?
choices: Create a Local Secondary Index (LSI) with customerId as partition key and orderDate as sort key
Create a Global Secondary Index (GSI) with orderStatus as partition key and orderDate as sort key
Create a Local Secondary Index (LSI) with customerId as partition key and orderStatus as sort key
Use a Scan operation with a FilterExpression for all queries
explanation_html:
Correct answer: Create a Local Secondary Index (LSI) with customerId as partition key and orderDate as sort key

An LSI shares the same partition key as the base table (customerId) but uses a different sort key (orderDate), enabling efficient range queries within a partition. LSIs must be created at table creation time. For filtering by orderStatus, you can use FilterExpression after retrieving sorted results. A GSI with orderStatus as partition key distributes data differently and would require scanning all orders of a status. A Scan with FilterExpression reads the entire table and is inefficient.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/LSI.html

question: A developer needs to generate a time-limited URL that allows an unauthenticated user to download a private object from S3. What should the developer use?
choices: S3 bucket policy with a condition on the IP address
S3 pre-signed URL generated with valid AWS credentials
CloudFront signed URL with an OAC
S3 access point with a public policy
explanation_html:
Correct answer: S3 pre-signed URL generated with valid AWS credentials

A pre-signed URL grants temporary access to a private S3 object. The URL is generated using the creator's credentials and includes an expiration time. Anyone with the URL can access the object until it expires, without needing AWS credentials. S3 bucket policies control access at the bucket level, not per-object time-limited access. CloudFront signed URLs are valid for distribution-level access control but require CloudFront setup. S3 access points with public policies would make the object permanently public.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/ShareObjectPreSignedURL.html

question: An SQS queue receives thousands of small messages per second. A Lambda function processes them in batches. Processing has been slow and some messages are expiring. What change will most improve throughput?
choices: Increase the SQS message retention period
Increase the Lambda batch size and enable batch window
Switch from a standard queue to a FIFO queue
Reduce the Lambda function memory allocation
explanation_html:
Correct answer: Increase the Lambda batch size and enable batch window

Increasing the batch size (up to 10,000 for standard queues) allows Lambda to process more messages per invocation, reducing overhead. The batch window setting (up to 300 seconds) allows Lambda to accumulate messages before invoking, improving efficiency for high-throughput scenarios. Increasing retention prevents expiry but does not improve throughput. FIFO queues have lower throughput limits than standard queues. Reducing memory decreases processing speed.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/with-sqs.html

question: A Lambda function occasionally receives malformed messages from SQS that cause it to fail. After several retries the messages should be moved aside for investigation without blocking processing. What should the developer configure?
choices: Set the SQS visibility timeout to 0 for failed messages
Configure a Dead Letter Queue (DLQ) on the SQS queue with a maxReceiveCount
Set the Lambda function reserved concurrency to handle retries
Enable SQS long polling to reduce failed message rate
explanation_html:
Correct answer: Configure a Dead Letter Queue (DLQ) on the SQS queue with a maxReceiveCount

A Dead Letter Queue receives messages that have been received more than the maxReceiveCount number of times without being successfully deleted. This isolates poison-pill messages for later inspection while allowing healthy messages to continue processing. Setting visibility timeout to 0 makes messages immediately visible, causing infinite retries. Reserved concurrency controls parallelism, not message failure handling. Long polling reduces empty receives but does not handle persistent failures.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/sqs-dead-letter-queues.html

question: A developer needs to ensure a Lambda function can handle a burst of 500 concurrent invocations for a critical payment processing service without being affected by other Lambda functions in the same account. What should be configured?
choices: Set the Lambda function timeout to the maximum value
Configure reserved concurrency of 500 on the function
Enable provisioned concurrency of 500 on the function
Increase the Lambda memory to the maximum value
explanation_html:
Correct answer: Configure reserved concurrency of 500 on the function

Reserved concurrency guarantees a set number of concurrent executions exclusively for a function, preventing it from being throttled by other functions and preventing it from consuming all account-level concurrency. Provisioned concurrency pre-warms execution environments to eliminate cold starts but does not reserve capacity away from other functions. Timeout controls execution duration, not concurrency. Memory affects performance, not concurrency limits.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/configuration-concurrency.html

question: A developer is uploading a 10 GB file to Amazon S3. The upload fails partway through due to a network error. What is the most efficient way to handle this scenario?
choices: Re-upload the entire file from the beginning after each failure
Use the S3 multipart upload API with checkpointing to resume failed parts
Compress the file below 5 GB before uploading to use the standard PUT API
Upload the file to EC2 first then copy to S3 using the AWS CLI
explanation_html:
Correct answer: Use the S3 multipart upload API with checkpointing to resume failed parts

S3 multipart upload splits a file into parts (minimum 5 MB each, up to 10,000 parts) that are uploaded independently. If a part fails, only that part needs to be retried, not the entire file. Multipart upload is required for objects larger than 5 GB and recommended for objects larger than 100 MB. Re-uploading the entire file is wasteful. Files over 5 GB cannot be uploaded with a single PUT request. Routing through EC2 adds unnecessary cost and latency.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/mpuoverview.html

question: A DynamoDB table has a partition key of userId and sort key of timestamp. A query retrieves all items for a userId. The developer notices strongly consistent reads are significantly more expensive than eventually consistent reads. When is a strongly consistent read required?
choices: When reading data that was written more than 1 second ago
When reading data immediately after a write and the application requires the latest value
When querying across multiple partitions
When using a Global Secondary Index
explanation_html:
Correct answer: When reading data immediately after a write and the application requires the latest value

DynamoDB strongly consistent reads return the most up-to-date data, reflecting all writes that received a successful response prior to the read. They are necessary when your application requires read-your-writes consistency — for example, reading immediately after writing. Eventually consistent reads may reflect slightly stale data (usually within one second). Strongly consistent reads are not required based on write age. GSIs only support eventually consistent reads, not strongly consistent. Cross-partition queries use the same consistency model per partition.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/HowItWorks.ReadConsistency.html

question: A developer needs to implement real-time processing of clickstream data from a website. The application must process records in the order they arrive per user session and replay data if needed. Which service is most appropriate?
choices: Amazon SQS Standard Queue
Amazon SQS FIFO Queue
Amazon Kinesis Data Streams
Amazon SNS with Lambda
explanation_html:
Correct answer: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams

Kinesis Data Streams provides ordered, replayable streams of records partitioned by a shard. Records in a shard are ordered and consumers can reprocess data by seeking to a specific position using sequence numbers or timestamps. Kinesis retains data for 24 hours by default (up to 365 days). SQS Standard queues do not guarantee ordering. SQS FIFO queues guarantee ordering but do not support replay. SNS is a pub/sub system without ordering or replay capabilities.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/streams/latest/dev/introduction.html
